name: PEEK-CF (Carbon-Fiber-Filled PEEK)
chemical_makeup: The same semi-crystalline polyaryletherketone backbone as the peek grade — aromatic rings joined by alternating ether and ketone linkages — compounded with chopped carbon fiber, disclosed at 10 wt% by 3DXTech (CarbonX PEEK+CF10). The fiber raises stiffness and, more usefully for printing, nucleates crystallisation more evenly, which is why the filled grade warps somewhat less than unfilled peek despite identical polymer chemistry.
summary: PEEK with the stiffness problem solved and the printability problem unchanged. Deltas vs the peek grade: tensile rises to 105-119 MPa, HDT climbs to 265 °C @0.45 MPa against ~145 °C unfilled, and warp eases slightly because the fiber nucleates crystallisation more evenly — paid for with a mandatory hardened nozzle, worse layer adhesion in Z, and a price around $715/kg. Everything else is unchanged and unforgiving: a 400 °C industrial hotend no consumer machine can reach, an actively heated 70-150 °C chamber that is genuinely mandatory, and a 120 °C drying cycle.

printing.notes: 3DXTech's 380-410 °C window is recorded and is consistent with the unfilled peek grade's 375-410 °C. Tectonic's KRATIR rPEEK CF listing gives 250-270 °C, which is roughly 140 °C below any plausible PEEK melt and is treated as a datasheet anomaly or a different process entirely rather than a competing specification (see conflicts). heated_chamber_required is true and means it: PEEK crystallises almost immediately on cooling and 70-150 °C ambient is what stands between a part and severe warp with delamination. Part cooling at or near zero for the same reason. A hardened nozzle is mandatory here where it is optional for unfilled peek — carbon fiber destroys brass — with 0.4 mm the practical minimum (Tectonic specifies 0.6 mm for its grade). This is industrial hardware only: the 400 °C requirement is above the X1E/H2D high-temp hotend's ~350 °C ceiling.

feeding.notes: Rigid and easy to push mechanically, but direct drive is strongly preferred — a long Bowden path fights the extrusion pressure needed at 400 °C with a fiber-loaded melt. AMS is a flat 'no' on two independent grounds: the process temperature is far outside any material station's range, and the 120 °C drying specification exceeds what an AMS-HT dryer delivers. Feed from a heated drybox on the industrial machine.

methods: print directly from a heated drybox
drying.dryness_validation: No popping, hissing or visible steam at the nozzle and no foaming in the purge — at 400 °C trace moisture flashes to steam violently, making the audible test unusually reliable. Extrudate should be a continuous strand, not a blistered one.
drying.notes: 3DXTech specifies 120 °C for 4 h, matching the unfilled peek grade exactly. Tectonic specifies 80 °C for 6-8 h for its recycled grade — 40 °C cooler and twice as long (see conflicts). Recorded 'always' and, as with unfilled PEEK, the practical rule is that the material is stored and printed from a dry box rather than dried once and left out: moisture that would merely string in PETG bubbles catastrophically at 400 °C.

storage.recommendations: Sealed with desiccant at all times and fed from a heated drybox during the print. Equilibrium moisture uptake is modest, but the consequence at 400 °C is severe, so the drybox is part of the machine rather than an accessory.

price.notes: Approximately $715/kg for the 3DXTech CarbonX PEEK+CF10 1 kg spool — a single-vendor datapoint. That sits within the unfilled peek grade's $400-900/kg band rather than above it, so the fiber loading does not carry a clear premium at this tier. The broader market band is unverified.

recommended: metal replacement where stiffness-to-weight is the driver
oil and gas downhole and sealing components
parts facing combined chemical attack and sustained high temperature
high-temperature jigs and tooling above what pei-ultem can hold
not_recommended: any consumer printer — 400 °C is above every stock and high-temp consumer hotend
parts loaded in Z — fiber reinforcement makes the anisotropy worse, not better
large flat geometry (immediate crystallisation drives warp even with a chamber)
prototyping and iteration — failed prints cost hundreds of dollars

properties.notes: HDT 265 °C at 0.45 MPa (3DXTech) against roughly 145 °C for the unfilled peek grade — the largest HDT gain from fiber loading anywhere in this catalog, and the main reason to choose the filled grade. Tectonic's recycled grade quotes 270 °C at the harsher 1.8 MPa load, which would be a stronger result still (see conflicts). Tensile 105-119 MPa. Tg 143 °C is unchanged from unfilled PEEK, as expected — fiber does not move the glass transition, only the load-bearing behaviour above it. Density 1.39 g/cm³ (Tectonic gives 1.36 for its grade), against 1.30 for unfilled peek, the expected increase from a ~10 wt% fiber loading. Melting point 343 °C carries over from the base grade. Shrinkage is not published and is left blank, but as with unfilled PEEK it is driven by near-immediate crystallisation rather than simple thermal contraction, which is what makes chamber control mandatory.

compatibility.notes: Inherits the base peek grade's position exactly. No soluble support chemistry survives anywhere near 380-410 °C — pva and bvoh degrade more than 200 °C below this window — so the options are self-supporting geometry or a breakaway PAEK interface. pekk is listed as a plausible breakaway support partner on shared PAEK chemistry and overlapping melt behaviour, carried over from the peek entry, but no source in this pass tested that interface for the filled grade specifically (unverified). It bonds to nothing in the commodity half of this catalog; pla, petg, abs, asa, pc, pa and pp are all destroyed on contact.

alternatives.reason: Unfilled PEEK at a similar or lower price with a better layer bond (adhesion 6 vs 4) and no hardened nozzle — giving up roughly 120 °C of HDT (145 vs 265 °C) and the stiffness that is the whole point of the filled grade.

The more printable member of the PAEK family at $495-700: 345-375 °C rather than 400 °C, better layer adhesion and less warp, with Tg 162 °C against 143 °C — but nothing like the filled grade's stiffness or its 265 °C HDT.

A fraction of the price ($172-266 vs ~$715) and printable on a good enclosed machine at 280-315 °C with no industrial hotend — HDT 227 °C gets surprisingly close, but continuous service and chemical resistance are not comparable, and PPA is far more moisture-sensitive.

emissions.notes: No PEEK-CF-specific VOC or particulate measurement was found. Carried from the unfilled peek entry, where the reasoning is that emission scales steeply with process temperature and 380-410 °C is near the top of this catalog's range, so ventilation is 'required' — enclosure plus external exhaust, or serious HEPA-plus-carbon filtration. VOC is 'moderate' rather than 'high' because PEEK is thermally stable within its own processing window. The one addition over the unfilled grade is post-processing carbon fiber dust, which is a respiratory hazard the unfilled material does not have. Both printing levels are inferred, not measured (unverified).

safety_notes: Abrasive: a hardened steel or ruby nozzle is mandatory and brass will not survive a spool. Wear respiratory protection with dust capture when sanding or machining printed parts — carbon fiber fines are a respiratory irritant. A 400 °C hotend, a 160 °C bed and a chamber holding 150 °C are all severe burn hazards, and the chamber must be allowed to cool and vent before the door is opened. Do not attempt to push a hotend beyond its rated temperature to reach these numbers. Not food-contact suitable: no certified grade was found and the fiber-roughened surface compounds the usual FDM layer-crevice problem.
additional_notes: Choose the filled grade over unfilled peek when stiffness or heat-under-load is the binding constraint, and accept that layer adhesion gets worse rather than better — design the part so the load never runs through Z. Tectonic's KRATIR rPEEK CF is notable as a 100 % recycled PEEK-CF feedstock, which is unusual at this tier, but its published process figures do not reconcile with any other PEEK source and should be checked directly with the vendor before use.

provenance.conflicts: The Tectonic KRATIR rPEEK CF listing disagrees with 3DXTech on four figures and one of them is not reconcilable. Nozzle: Tectonic lists 250-270 °C against 3DXTech's 380-410 °C — roughly 140 °C apart and far below the 343 °C melting point of PEEK, so it is treated as a datasheet anomaly or a listing for a materially different process rather than a competing specification; 3DXTech is treated as authoritative throughout. Density: 1.39 (3DXTech) against 1.36 (Tectonic); 1.39 is recorded and the derived weight/volume figures follow it. HDT: 265 °C @0.45 MPa (3DXTech) against 270 °C @1.8 MPa (Tectonic) — different load conditions, not directly comparable, and the 3DXTech figure is recorded because it matches the load condition used elsewhere in this catalog. Drying: 120 °C / 4 h (3DXTech) against 80 °C / 6-8 h (Tectonic). Minimum nozzle diameter: 0.4 mm (3DXTech) against 0.6 mm (Tectonic). Price rests on one 3DXTech 1 kg listing. Fiber loading is disclosed only by 3DXTech (10 wt%). Emissions are inferred from the unfilled peek entry with no measurement for either grade. The pekk breakaway-support pairing is reasoned from shared PAEK chemistry and was not tested for the filled grade.

trade_names.notes: 10 wt% chopped carbon fiber; the source of this entry's recorded figures (380-410 °C, HDT 265 °C @0.45 MPa, density 1.39).
100 % recycled PEEK-CF feedstock. Published figures diverge sharply from 3DXTech's, including a 250-270 °C nozzle range below PEEK's melting point (see conflicts).
